macro: The Fed held its policy rate at 3.50%-3.75% on July 29 in a 9-3 vote, with Chair Kevin Warsh calling the case for a September move 'finely balanced.' June CPI cooled to 3.5% year-over-year (core 2.6%) and core PCE ran at 3.3%, while a U.S.-Iran interim deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz has eased oil-driven inflation risk this week. This week's data has been mixed: ISM Manufacturing surged to 55.6%, a four-year high, even as JOLTS job openings fell to 7.36 million and ADP private payrolls rose just 44,000 in July, the weakest pace since January. The single most important event to watch: today's nonfarm payrolls report at 8:30am ET, the last major labor read before the Fed's September 16 meeting.
btc_status: Bitcoin trades near $64,600, essentially flat and holding just above its roughly $63,770 200-week moving average, the support level that has marked every bear-market low since 2015. Alternative.me's Fear & Greed reading could not be independently confirmed today, with third-party trackers split between fear and neutral; the level to watch is $63,000 support against $66,800 resistance, the range that has bounded price for weeks.

energy: WTI crude trades near $77.20, roughly flat on the session, while Brent sits near $82.15, down about 0.4%, as the U.S.-Iran interim deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz continues to ease the geopolitical premium. The EIA's most recent report (week ended July 31, released Aug 5) showed commercial crude inventories rose 2.5 million barrels to 407.0 million, a build that ran counter to analyst expectations of a draw. A durable Hormuz agreement remains the key swing factor for prices into next week.
vix_and_dollar: The VIX closed near 15.3 on Thursday, in the calm-to-normal range, while the DXY sits near 99.98, up slightly and firming for a second straight session. The combination — subdued volatility alongside a strengthening dollar — points to markets holding a cautious, wait-and-see posture ahead of today's jobs report.
mortgage_rate: The 30-year fixed mortgage averaged 6.69% in Freddie Mac's August 6 survey, up from 6.66% the week prior and its sixth increase in seven weeks. Mortgage applications fell 2.9% over the same period, per the Mortgage Bankers Association, as rising rates continue to offset the affordability gains from wage growth earlier this year.
personal_finance_deep_dive: Student loan delinquencies reached 10.3% of balances 90 or more days past due in the first quarter, up from 9.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and the highest share since 2020, according to the New York Fed. The increase traces directly to the resumption of federal loan payments in October 2024 after a multi-year pandemic pause, which left many borrowers unprepared for bills that had been suspended for years. Younger borrowers and those who took on debt without completing a degree are showing the sharpest deterioration, since they tend to carry smaller balances but far less income cushion to absorb a new monthly payment. The trend is an early warning sign for consumer credit broadly, since student loan delinquencies have historically preceded stress showing up in auto and card data.
wealth_building_deep_dive: Fidelity's Q1 2026 retirement analysis found the average 401(k) employee savings rate reached 9.6%, the highest on record, pushing the total savings rate (employee plus employer match) to a record 14.4%. IRA contributions were up 29% year-over-year, driven largely by Roth accounts, which captured 67% of new contributions as savers increasingly prioritize tax-free growth over an upfront deduction. The mechanism working in savers' favor is largely automatic: auto-enrollment and auto-escalation features have pushed contribution rates higher without requiring an active decision each year. A concrete step this week: anyone who hasn't checked their contribution rate against their plan's full employer match should do so, since a partial match left on the table is a guaranteed return no market can match.
